activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: One of Amazon's leadership principles, 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit', asks employees to respectfully challenge a decision they disagree with, then commit fully once it is made.
story:
The email arrived on a Thursday, three days after the engineering club's fall showcase planning meeting, and Henry read it four times at the kitchen counter before he touched anything on his plate. Mr. Islam's message was short, its paragraphs like stacked bricks: the decision, the reasoning, the deadline. The club's app would go to the showcase as a water-usage tracker for the school building, not as the campus marketplace Henry had spent two months designing, the one where students could trade leftover meal points so the food wouldn't just commodify into numbers on a card that expired in June. Water it was. The decision, the email said, was final for this semester.

Henry typed a reply that night, and it took him two hours to produce six sentences, most of the work being deletion. His first draft called the decision "insane." His second called it "a waste of everyone's September." Both went into the trash, and he noticed himself noticing that: the difference between what he felt and what he could send. What he finally sent laid out three reasons, numbered, with a line of acknowledgment at the top, that the meal-point marketplace had already drawn interest from forty students in his survey, that the water tracker duplicated an existing district dashboard, and that he was willing to present his data at any time convenient. He read it aloud once, quietly, the way you test whether a sentence can survive being said to someone's face.

Mr. Islam answered the next morning. Henry read it in the stairwell before first period, phone held low against his binder. The reply matched his structure point for point, numbered, unhurried, and it dismantled him. The district dashboard, Mr. Islam wrote, was three years stale and nobody used it; the water tracker would be live. The survey, he noted gently, measured interest in free food, not interest in maintaining a marketplace over eight months. At the bottom: "I appreciate the tone of your note, Henry. This is how to disagree. The decision stands, and I'd like you to lead the build." Henry stared at the last line for a long moment, because it was somehow worse than a plain refusal. He had been heard, and he had lost anyway.

He didn't lead the build, at first. He went to Amir's house after school and sat on the floor of the garage with a can of root beer going warm beside him, explaining the whole thing with his hands while Amir sorted bolts into a tackle box. Amir had his own stake in the showcase; his older brother had won it two years ago and their father still kept the trophy on top of the fridge, and Amir wanted his name on something of his own, not a component, not "assisted by." He listened all the way to the end, which was unusual for him, and then he said, "My sister works at Amazon. She says they have this thing, one of their leadership principles, it's called 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit.' You respectfully challenge a decision you disagree with, then commit fully once it's made." He shook the tackle box to settle the bolts. "So what's the commit part look like for you?"

Henry said he didn't know, which was true, and they worked on Amir's drivetrain until dark, the garage light drawing moths against the door. The reprieve of the mechanical work, the way a stripped gear could be fixed with hands instead of arguments, lasted until he was walking home and found himself drafting a second email in his head, the capitulating kind, the kind that agrees in a way that makes sure everyone knows it hurts. He stopped on the sidewalk and deleted the draft in his head sentence by sentence. That wasn't committing. That was sulking in a business suit.

The email he sent on Sunday was three sentences. He would lead the build. He had an idea about the sensors that might cut cost by a third. Could he come Tuesday at lunch. Mr. Islam replied with a single line, "Tuesday works," and nothing else, and Henry found the brevity strangely steadying, like a hand on the shoulder that doesn't grip.

Tuesday at lunch, the physics room smelled of dry-erase marker and someone's microwave noodles. Mr. Islam had printed Henry's original email and his own reply and set them side by side on the lab table. "Keep these," he said. "You'll write a lot of these in college. Most people learn at twenty-five and it costs them a job." Then he rolled out the sensor diagrams and it was just work, honest work, and Henry's cost-cutting idea was accepted in the first ten minutes, without ceremony, which he understood was itself a kind of ceremony.

The build took five weeks. Henry put in more hours than the marketplace had ever gotten from him, and he couldn't decide, walking to Amir's garage on the final Friday with the tracker finished in his backpack, whether that was growth or just the habit of a person who does the next thing well because he doesn't know how to do it badly. Amir had won his own small war; the presentation slides would credit him with the live data feed, his name, not a footnote. They tested the app in the garage, the water numbers ticking upward in real time, and it was genuinely good, and it was not the thing Henry had wanted, and both of those facts sat in him side by side without merging.

At the showcase, a judge from the utility company spent ten minutes at their table and asked Henry why he'd chosen water. "I didn't," Henry said. "I argued against it, in writing, and I lost." The judge raised an eyebrow, and Amir laughed, and somewhere behind them Mr. Islam was talking to another team, and Henry turned the tablet so the graph faced the light.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940), the dead hummingbird hanging at her throat is a Mexican folk charm for luck in love.
story:
The assignment was due Friday, and Matthew had typed three sentences and deleted four. Mr. Menon had taped a print of the Kahlo to the whiteboard, Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, 1940, and told them flatly that "I like the colours" would earn them nothing. Formal analysis, he kept saying, as if the words themselves were a door he could shove them through. Colour, composition, symbolism. Matthew had written those three words at the top of his notebook and then sat there while the room filled with the smell of turpentine and Garrett's whispering.

Khalil leaned across the table, tapping the bird hanging at the painter's throat. "It's dead, though. Look at it. Wings out, eyes shut. So it's like, death at her neck, right? She's saying love kills you or whatever." He had a whole theory already, something trenchant about the thorns drawing blood and the monkey tugging the ribbon, and Matthew could hear the teacher nodding at it from here. Khalil could talk like that, could make a paragraph sound like an argument, and it worked on people. It had worked on Matthew for years.

But Matthew kept circling back to the bird. The rest of the painting supported Khalil's reading, more or less. The thorns bit her skin, the cat watched with flat intent, the background leaves pressed in like a wall. Yet the hummingbird bothered him, and he couldn't say why except that it hung there like a pendant. Dead things weren't pendants. Dead things were dead. People wore pendants for luck, for protection, for wanting something.

Garrett, two tables over, was building his essay on the hummingbird too. "Decoration," he said when Matthew asked him. "She just liked the shape. Artists put stuff in because it looks cool." Garrett believed, generally, that everything was either cool or not cool, a kind of meritocracy of images where the best-looking ones won, and Matthew had spent most of high school finding this comfortable and only lately finding it thin. He said nothing now. He copied the painting onto his phone and looked at it on the bus, on his bed, at dinner until his mother told him to put it away.

Khalil's grandmother came on Thursday afternoon. She was picking Khalil up from detention makeup, and she drifted into the art room while the three of them stayed late, on the pretext of borrowing the good scissors. She stood in front of the print with her coat still buttoned and her reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and she touched the edge of the paper, not the image, the paper, as though it were a doorway. Khalil said, "Abuela, it's for our essay," and she looked at the hummingbird for a long moment and laughed, a small surprised sound.

"That's a charm," she said. "In Mexico they hang the little dead bird for luck in love."

Matthew's pen stopped. She said something else in Spanish, softer, and Khalil translated it as her mother keeping one in a matchbox, and then she patted Khalil's arm and went to wait by the car. The room was quiet after. Garrett said, "Luck in love? But it's dead," and that was exactly it, that was the thing Matthew had been circling for three days. She wears a dead bird to ask for love. The painting wasn't arguing one thing. It was holding two.

He wrote the essay that night anyway, because it was due. He laid out the composition first, the flat frontal stare, the symmetrical animals flanking her like a votive image, the foliage closing off any distance between her and the viewer. He described the palette, the wet greens and the blood reds bleeding into each other. Then he built his paragraph around the charm, around the fact that a wish for love could be carried by something already dead, and that Kahlo painted it the year after her divorce became final and public and humiliating, though he cut that last part because Mr. Menon wanted analysis, not biography, and because he couldn't prove what she wanted.

He read Khalil's essay before class, because Khalil had asked him to. It was good. It was sharp and it moved, and it took the bird as an emblem of love's cruelty, and there was nothing in it that was wrong exactly. Matthew sat with both versions in his head, his and Khalil's, and could not make them into one thing. Maybe they weren't one thing. Maybe the charm meant both at once, the way a wound means the body healing and the body hurt, and he could not write that sentence without hearing how it sounded, so he left it out.

Mr. Menon handed the essays back on Monday with a single comment on each. On Matthew's he had written, in blue pen, "You resist your own conclusion. Good. See me." On Khalil's: "Persuasive." Khalil grinned and held it up across the room. Matthew looked at his own, then at the print still hanging by the window, the little bird swinging on nothing at the painter's throat, wings open, going nowhere.

"See me," Matthew read aloud.

"So go," Khalil said, and picked up his print, already halfway out the door.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Psychologist Robert Zajonc's 1968 experiments showed the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else, and Alexia stood in the middle of the living room holding a box marked KITCHEN, MISC, unsure where the kitchen even was. Her mother's voice carried from somewhere above, calling out measurements for curtains. Through the uncurtained window the street ran straight and identical, house after house the same beige, and at the far end she could see the bus stop where the number 14 would carry her to a school she had not yet entered.

She set the box down and texted Kian a photo of the empty room, floorboards bare, one overhead bulb. "looks like a crime scene," he wrote back, and then, three minutes later, "u ok?" She did not answer that one. It was easier to answer the joke.

The movers had expropriated the driveway with their truck, and one of them kept asking her where things should go, as if she had any authority here, as if she had chosen any of it. She pointed at corners more or less at random. Her desk ended up under a window that faced the neighbor's fence, and when she sat on the floor beside it, the silence was so complete she could hear her own swallowing.

That first week she rode the 14 to school and hated it with a specific, detailed hatred. The route looped past a strip mall, a fertilizer plant, a chain-link yard full of municipal trucks, and it took forty minutes to cover a distance that should have taken fifteen. She told Ryland, the only person who had spoken to her twice, that the bus was designed as a punishment. "It grows on you," Ryland said, slurping the dregs of a cafeteria smoothie. "I used to think so too. Now I kind of like it." Alexia privately classified this as a defect in Ryland's character.

At night she called Kian, and the calls got shorter. Not because of anything anyone said. It was only that a call about nothing needs a shared nothing, and they no longer had the same one. He told a story about their old chemistry teacher, whose erudition had always leaked out in strange directions, tangents on alchemy, on the history of glass, and Alexia laughed at the right place and then could not remember, afterward, whether she had actually found it funny.

In the school library, killing a free period, she opened a psychology textbook someone had left on the returns cart, not because she was interested but because the alternative was her phone. She read a page, then the page again. In 1968, an experimenter named Robert Zajonc had shown people nonsense shapes and faces they had never seen, and the ones shown more often were the ones they liked better. People tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often. It was called the mere-exposure effect. She sat very still with her hand flat on the page, the way you press on a bruise to check it.

Because here was the thing. It was late October now, and she had ridden the 14 for seven weeks, and somewhere in there the route had stopped being a punishment. The fertilizer plant had a slanted roof where pigeons clustered at exactly the same time each morning, diurnal as anything, and the municipal yard had a gate that squealed on a note she had begun to find almost musical. She had noticed herself noticing. She did not know what to do with that. It could mean the place was genuinely becoming hers, or it could mean her judgment was just wearing down, the way a stone wears down, and there was no instrument she knew of that could tell the two apart.

She tried the idea out on Ryland at the bus stop, the wind shoving at both of them. "Zajonc found people like things more just from seeing them more. Mere exposure." Ryland squinted down the empty road. "So my liking this bus stop is basically a lab result." "It's from 1968," Alexia said. "So it's a very old lab result." Ryland considered this. "That actually makes me feel better. If it happened to people in 1968, at least it's not just me being weak."

But that wasn't quite it either, and she knew it, standing there with her collar up. Kian had seen her thousands of times and had still gone quiet on the phone, so exposure wasn't a law, it was a tendency, a lean. Maybe the liking was real and also manufactured, and maybe those were not different things. She held both possibilities the way she now held the bus pole every morning, loosely, without demanding that it mean anything.

On Saturday she unpacked the last box, books this time, and shelved them wrong on purpose, alphabetical order abandoned, because the room was new and she could. From the window the identical beige houses ran on down the street, and she recognized them now, all of them, which proved nothing and which she decided, for today, to let count. She picked up her phone and texted Kian a photo of the full shelf. "come see it eventually," she wrote, and then the 14 went by at the corner, empty and lit, on its way to somewhere it already knew.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
The instructor, Mr. Suryanto, was already standing in the driveway when Brandon came out, and he was not alone. A girl Brandon recognized from the next street over, a junior, sat in the driver's seat of the training car with her hands folded in her lap, and Mr. Suryanto stood beside the open door with one palm resting on the roof. He wasn't raising his voice. He wasn't saying anything at all. That was somehow worse.

"She forgot her belt," Yannick said from the porch steps across the street, where he'd set himself up with a slushie to watch. "In the driveway. Not even moving. And he pulled the keys."

"She has to click it and then he'll start the lesson," Steven said, arriving late and out of breath, as if the information itself had to be delivered quickly. "My sister had him last year. He did the same thing."

The girl buckled the belt. Mr. Suryanto still didn't move. He leaned down and said something too quiet for Brandon to hear, and she answered, and he straightened up and looked at his watch. Then he walked around to the passenger side, got in, and the car rolled backward out of the driveway with the careful, painful slowness of a first lesson, the girl's hands at ten and two, her head swiveling at nothing.

"That's insane," Yannick said. "She was parked. You can't die in a driveway."

"It's not about the driveway," Brandon said, and then found he didn't know what it was about, exactly, and stood there holding the sentence.

They waited on the curb, the three of them, because Brandon's lesson came next, the second slot of the morning, and Mr. Suryanto was nothing if not punctual. The street was quiet in the way suburbs are quiet on a Saturday: a sprinkler ticking somewhere, a garage door half open, the incipient hum of lawnmowers that would start in another hour once everyone finished breakfast. Steven kept checking his phone. Yannick kept narrating the training car's progress down the block, two miles an hour past Mrs. Okafor's hedges, a full stop at the empty stop sign as though it were the border of a country.

When the car returned and the girl got out, her face was flushed but composed, and Mr. Suryanto shook her hand once, formally, the way you'd close a business deal. Then he looked over at the curb and beckoned.

Brandon got in. He adjusted the mirror, checked the mirror, put his foot on the brake before touching the key, all the things the manual had said and his mother had drilled into him at the kitchen table with a paper plate for a steering wheel. He reached for the belt last. And he paused, deliberately, long enough that Mr. Suryanto noticed the pause.

"You wanted to ask something," Mr. Suryanto said. It wasn't a question.

"My friend thinks the belt thing in the driveway was overkill." Brandon clicked it. "I think he's kind of right and kind of wrong and I can't split the difference."

Mr. Suryanto took out a folded sheet of statistics from the visor, the way another man might produce a map, and set it on the dashboard without handing it over. "Read the third line when you're stopped. Not now. Now you drive."

They drove. Brandon's turns were wide and his braking was abrupt and twice Mr. Suryanto said "brake" in a tone so flat it functioned as a whole lecture. At the four-way stop where nobody was waiting, Mr. Suryanto made him do the full sequence anyway, and Brandon began to understand that the man's severity in the driveway was not severity at all but architecture, a set of habits meant to underpin everything that came after, poured before the concrete set. Yannick's position, he thought, was that rules should be proportionate to danger, that treating a parked car like a highway was a kind of dishonesty. Mr. Suryanto's position was that you didn't get to choose which moments mattered, that the habit had to be older than the judgment. Both of them were arguing about the same thing from opposite ends, and Brandon, steering around a recycling bin someone had left too close to the curb, could not decide which end he lived on.

Back in his own driveway, engine off, he read the third line. It said that according to the CDC, wearing a seat belt cut serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. He read it twice. About half. Not eliminated, not promised, just halved, and he sat with the strange shape of that number, the way it offered something and withheld something at the same time.

"So was it worth it?" he asked. "Making her do it in the driveway. Half of a driveway is nothing."

"Half of a highway is a great deal," Mr. Suryanto said, taking the sheet back and folding it along its old creases. "You never know which one you're sitting in until afterward."

Brandon pulled the belt off slowly. He thought about saying that that logic could justify anything, that Yannick would call it superstition dressed as arithmetic, that Steven's sister had apparently survived a year of it and still texted while driving. He thought about saying he agreed. He did neither, because neither was quite true, and Mr. Suryanto was already out of the car and writing something on his clipboard.

Across the street, Yannick cupped his hands around his mouth. "Did he yell at you about the belt?"

Brandon held up the clipboard moment with two fingers, no idea what the man had written, probably "wide turns," probably something worse. "Ask me in ten years," he called back, and stood up out of the car still holding the belt strap, letting it rewind slowly through his fingers.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister.
story:
The projector hummed while Ms. Hu wrote "SOURCES" on the board and underlined it twice, and Jasmine copied the word into her notebook without looking down. In the second row, Andre had his tablet open to a news site, tilting the screen toward Lauriane.

"See, this is why nobody trusts anything," he said. "This piece on the strike, it's two paragraphs long and the union guy gets one quote."

Lauriane leaned away from the screen. "So find a longer piece somewhere else. That's the whole point of the assignment."

Jasmine turned around in her seat. "It's not just about length. Who wrote it matters less than who signs the paycheques."

"Here we go," Andre said.

Ms. Hu clapped her hands once. "Pairs. Pick one outlet each and trace who owns it. I want the chain, not the name. Parent company, then whoever owns that." She moved between the desks before anyone could ask her anything more, which was her way of saying the work belonged to them.

Jasmine pulled her chair next to Andre's. He was already sulking at his tablet. "This is going to turn into you lecturing me about capitalism."

"Only if you keep calling it lecturing." She typed the outlet's name into the search bar and followed the ownership links down, page by page, the way Ms. Hu had shown them in September. Two clicks in, the trail crossed a border. The parent company was Italian, and the name of its controlling shareholder made her stop.

"Andre. Look at this."

He looked. Then he looked again. "That can't be right."

"Silvio Berlusconi," she read. "He kept control of Mediaset while he was prime minister. Mediaset owns three of Italy's main national TV channels." She scrolled to confirm it on a second page, then a third, because it seemed like the kind of thing a search engine would hand you back wrong.

Lauriane had drifted over from her own desk, arms folded. "So what? Lots of rich people own stuff."

"He was the prime minister," Andre said. "That's what. The guy running the country owned the TV channels." He was quiet for a second, and Jasmine watched him actually sit with it. "Three of the main national ones."

"Would it bother you if a politician you liked did it?" Jasmine asked.

"That's not fair."

"It's the only question that matters."

Lauriane dropped into the empty chair on Jasmine's other side. "Okay, but flip it. Say you ban them from owning anything. Then only people who are already rich and not in politics own the channels, and they still shape the coverage, they just do it quieter. At least this way you know."

"That's not a feature," Andre said. "That's a bug wearing a hat."

"Everything's a bug wearing a hat if you don't like the hat."

Ms. Hu passed behind them, paused, read the screen over Andre's shoulder, and said only, "Good find," before moving on. Jasmine felt oddly cheated by that. She had wanted someone to tell her what to think about it, and Ms. Hu kept refusing, the way she refused every morning, standing at the board with her marker like a person guarding a door she would not open for you.

Jasmine pulled out a sheet of paper and drew a line down the middle. On the left she wrote what Lauriane had said, more or less: disclosure, knowing where it comes from, treating every outlet as interested. On the right she wrote Andre's side: a leader shouldn't sit on the megaphone, no matter which side of the line he's on. Under both, she wrote the thing neither of them had said out loud, which was that the chain she'd traced for their Canadian outlet was probably clean-looking too, probably, and she hadn't gotten to the bottom of it, and might not by Friday.

"You're doing the face," Andre said.

"What face?"

"The one where you think both of us are wrong and you're not going to say it."

"I think you're both right, which is worse." She turned the sheet toward him. "He shouldn't have owned them. And knowing he did is worth something. Both of those can be true and I don't know how to weight them yet. If I put this in the presentation, it's going to sound like I'm hedging."

"Then hedge with confidence," Lauriane said. "It's a very marketable skill."

The bell hadn't rung yet. Ms. Hu was erasing the board, the word SOURCES going first, the underline last. Jasmine copied the ownership chain onto a fresh index card, one name per line, and at the bottom wrote Berlusconi's name twice, once as shareholder and once as prime minister, then drew a small arrow between the two.

"That arrow is your whole presentation," Andre said, reading over her shoulder.

"It's one arrow," Jasmine said. "It's not the whole anything." She put the card in her binder and closed the clasp on it.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, the first movement's recapitulation begins unusually in F major, the subdominant, instead of the home key of C major.
story:
The program note called it a masterclass for listeners, but really it was a workshop: forty students in the upstairs rehearsal room of the concert hall, each with a photocopied score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, and two hours to mark its form before the recital downstairs. Ms. Watanabe, who ran the series, had explained the ground rules once, briskly, and then left them alone with the music. Exposition, development, recapitulation. Find them, mark them, defend them. Jessica had until intermission to slide her annotated pages into the folder by the door.

She had learned the textbook version, where a sonata movement lays out its themes in the exposition, tears them apart in the development, and brings them home in the recapitulation. That much she trusted. What she trusted less was her own ear, which was good in the way a borrowed tool is good: functional, unfamiliar in the hand. Teagan, on her left, had already drawn a thick red line at the return of the first theme and was leaning back with the satisfaction of someone finished early. Misha, on her right, kept wiggling her pencil above the page without committing it to paper.

"Where did you put yours?" Teagan asked.

"Where the tune comes back," Jessica said, and pointed to the same measure, which showed the first theme over a harmony Teagan had labeled C major without checking. It looked right. The melody was there, whole and cheerful, exactly where a recapitulation belonged.

Misha leaned across. "That's not a C in the bass, though." She played the beat on the room's upright piano, then the same phrase transposed, and the difference sat in the air between them like a smell neither could name. Teagan frowned and pressed her pencil eraser against her red line, but didn't lift it.

They were asked to leave the piano and take their seats, and Jessica carried her unmarked score down the wide carpeted stairs into the hall itself, where the audience murmured and settled and the lights found the pianist already sitting. Her pencil was warm in her hand. She had decided, on the stairs, on a small dishonesty: she would mark the recapitulation where the theme returned, in the ordinary place, and if the bass note was strange she would simply not write a key under it. It was the kind of decision that could underwrite a whole career of half-seeing, she thought, and then thought that was a dramatic way to put it, and kept her pencil ready anyway.

The performance began with the first movement. She knew the opening theme now the way you know a classmate's face, and she followed the exposition with small ticks in the margin, the second theme arriving in the expected key like a guest coming in through the front door. Then the development, which behaved the way her textbook promised, everything restless and dissolving. Her pencil hovered over the measure Teagan had chosen. Here it came. The first theme returned, note for note, and her wrist started to move, and then her ear did something her eye had refused to do: it registered the ground under the melody. The theme was home, and the ground was not. It was F major, one step to the left of where home should have been, and it stayed there for a while before the music found its way back to C, later, as if returning from an errand no one had announced.

She did not mark the line. Instead she wrote, in the margin, in handwriting she hoped Ms. Watanabe could read, that the recapitulation begins in F major in this movement, not in the home key of C, and that she had nearly put her line in the wrong place for the right reason. Around her the hall listened to the slow movement, and Teagan, three seats down, was erasing something, the friction of it faintly audible. Misha caught Jessica's eye across the row and mouthed, F major, and Jessica nodded once.

During intermission she stood by the folder near the door, her pages in her hand, and found Ms. Watanabe checking the biscuits table. "Mine's late," Jessica said. "I marked the recapitulation twice. Once where I wanted it, once where it is."

Ms. Watanabe took the pages, looked at the double line, one ghost and one solid, and said nothing, which Jessica chose to take as permission. Behind them, in the emptying hall, a piano tuner was already at work, and the first note he struck was a C.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows, so 100 customers and 1,000 orders produce 100,000 rows.
story:
The laptop belonged to Kingsley's older brother, and Kingsley had made Juliette promise twice not to install anything on it. "It's just a browser thing," she said, pulling her chair up to the kitchen table where the late light came through the blinds in stripes. "A sandbox. Nothing touches his files." Kingsley watched her type with the wariness of someone lending a pet to a stranger, and Harman, who had claimed the good armchair an hour ago, didn't even open his eyes.

The assignment had come from Ms. Nur, who taught the afternoon computer science elective and had a habit of setting problems that sounded like riddles. Two tables, she had said, customers and orders. Find the customers who ordered nothing. Harman had insisted it was a trick question, that nobody ordered nothing, and Kingsley had spent the walk home arguing that the point was the shape of the answer, not the answer itself. Juliette had said nothing on the walk, because the truth was she had a reason for wanting those names that had nothing to do with the assignment.

She built the tables first, in the browser window, filling them the way Ms. Nur had shown them: one hundred customers, which took three tedious paste operations, and a thousand orders drawn from a generated list. "A thousand," Kingsley said, reading over her shoulder. "That's a lot of orders. Who are these people?" "Nobody," Juliette said. "They're practice." That wasn't quite honest either, but she let it stand.

The query itself seemed simple enough. SELECT, the names, FROM customers, and then she typed JOIN orders, and in her hurry to see results she hit Enter before her fingers found the ON keyword. The tab went still. Then a thin bar at the bottom began to count, and count, and keep counting, past ten thousand, past fifty, and the fan inside the laptop climbed to a note like a kettle deciding whether to boil. "What did you do," Kingsley said, not as a question. "Nothing," Juliette said, which was exactly and catastrophically true.

Harman came out of his chair. The three of them stood in the striped light watching numbers accumulate, and the whole machine slowed until the cursor dragged across the screen like something moving through honey. "Kill it," Kingsley said, and reached for the power button, and Juliette caught his wrist. "Wait. Wait. I want to see how far it goes." "You're beseeching me to let it run?" Kingsley said, and she supposed she was, her hand light on his arm, her eyes on the count. Harman, arms folded, said, "One hundred customers. One thousand orders." He said it flatly, like reading a receipt, and then he said the number the count had just passed, and Juliette felt the shape of the thing arrive in her head all at once.

"Every customer against every order," she said slowly. "Every combination. A hundred customers and a thousand orders, and it's building a hundred thousand rows." The bar confirmed it, crawling toward that figure with terrible patience. She had written a join with no matching condition, and the database had taken her literally, matching nothing, combining everything, and a hundred thousand rows was apparently enough to make a healthy laptop behave like a dilettante pretending at hard labor. "So that's what the ON is for," she said. "It's not decoration. It's the fence."

She let go of Kingsley's wrist and closed the tab, and the fan wound down through its registers until the kitchen was quiet enough to hear the refrigerator. Kingsley exhaled. Harman said, "You could have told us you didn't know what ON did," and Juliette said, "I didn't not know. I just hadn't needed to know until now." This distinction satisfied her more than it satisfied either of them, and she could see Kingsley deciding whether it was worth arguing. He decided against it and slid the laptop back across the table toward her, which she took as a kind of absolution.

The second query she wrote carefully, almost ceremonially, with the ON clause in place and then, at the end, the part Ms. Nur had hinted at without naming: a condition asking for rows where no order existed. She ran it. The result came back in less than a second, a short clean list of customer names, and at the top of it, third from the beginning, was Kingsley's family name.

She had put their street's households in as sample customers days ago, telling herself it was only data, only practice, only a way to make the numbers feel real. She had not put in their orders. Kingsley's mother ran the shop at the corner, the one that had been empty most afternoons since spring, and Juliette had told herself she was building a problem about a database when she was building a question about a friend. She looked at the name on the screen and understood that she had been profligate with other people's information, spending it to satisfy her own curiosity, and that no query could tell her what to do with what she'd found.

"You get the answer?" Kingsley asked, leaning over. His eyes moved down the list, and she watched them, waiting to see where they stopped.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
Hayden had promised the drama club a backdrop for their end-of-year show, and what he had so far was a four-by-eight sheet of plywood leaning against the fence, painted with a hallway that looked like a hallway drawn by someone who had never walked down one. The lockers ran parallel, the floor ran parallel, the ceiling ran parallel, and the whole thing sat on the wood like a diagram, flat as a poster tacked to a wall. He knelt in the grass with a pencil behind his ear and a brush he was not using, and the deadline sat in his chest like a swallowed stone.

Finley came through the side gate carrying two iced teas and a folding chair, which he opened with the certainty of a man claiming territory. He had appointed himself assistant three days ago, though so far his assistance consisted of commentary and hydration. "It looks like a jail," he said, handing Hayden a cup. "A jail in a country with no building codes."

"It's a school hallway."

"It's a bad hallway. No offense. Offense. Some offense."

Ethen arrived next, bicycle helmet still on, because Ethen believed helmets were a lifestyle rather than equipment. He stood in front of the plywood with his head tilted, and Hayden watched him tilt, and waited, because Ethen's tilting head was the most reliable critic in the county. "Everything's going the same way," Ethen said finally. "The floor and the ceiling. They're both just straight across. That's why it's flat. Real halls, the floor comes toward you."

Hayden had been staring at the thing for two hours without being able to name that, and hearing it said aloud was like someone switching on a light in a room he'd been bumping around in. He picked up the pencil and, working fast before the idea could evaporate, drew a small mark in the center of the board, low, where a person's eye would fall. Then he angled the floor line to run down toward it, and the ceiling line to run up toward it, and the locker edges inward, all of them converging like roads on a map.

Finley stood, which for Finley was practically applause. "Whoa. It's deep. It looks like you could walk in."

"It's called linear perspective," Hayden said, half to himself. "Brunelleschi. Around 1420, in Florence. He demonstrated it. All the lines meet at one point, a vanishing point, and the flat surface shows depth." He had done a report on the Renaissance in tenth grade and copied most of it from a website, but the copying had left things behind in him, the way a flood leaves silt, and now here it was, useful. The board was no longer a hallway lying down. It was a hallway going somewhere, and the somewhere was a point the size of a pencil eraser.

Mr. Korhonen looked over the fence a little after five, drawn out, Hayden suspected, by the smell of turpentine and the sound of Finley arguing with a level. He was a retired draftsman who treated the neighborhood as a municipal jurisdiction he still served. He studied the board in silence for longer than was comfortable. "You discovered that on your own," he said, not quite a question.

"Ethen said the lines were wrong. I fixed it."

"Hm." Mr. Korhonen said it the way other men said congratulations. He pointed at the vanishing mark with a finger that had spent forty years pointing at drawings. "Now the problem is that it's correct and it's empty. A hallway nobody would walk down." Then he went back inside, having paid the exact amount of attention he intended to.

They painted until the mosquitoes came up from the hedge, Ethen holding a work lamp from his mother's garage, Finley narrating in the voice of a nature documentary, "Here we observe the artist in his suburban habitat, consuming his third iced tea." Hayden painted the floor darker as it went back, because he had noticed, crouching in the real hallway at school with his phone camera out like an idiot, that distance swallowed light. The vanishing point became a soft gray nothing, and somehow that nothing was the most convincing part. The project had captivated him in a way the actual play never had; he was sanguine about the actors forgetting their lines and the director hating the color of the lockers, because the board itself had done the one thing he'd asked it to do. Though even now, standing back under the lamp, he could not have said whether he had made art or just a very good illusion, and whether there was a difference, and he suspected the difference mattered and he suspected he would not resolve it before Friday.

Finley wanted his name on it somewhere, small, near the bottom, and had been lobbying for this since Tuesday. "Assistant to the artist," he proposed. "Curatorial consultant. I held the lamp."

"You held your tea. Ethen held the lamp."

"Emotional support," Finley said. "That's the leitmotif of my whole contribution. Emotional support, repeated throughout."

Hayden dipped a thin brush in white paint and, in the corner where the wall met the floor, where almost no one would look, wrote F + E in letters small as the vanishing point. Finley leaned in, found it, and said nothing for a full three seconds, which was a record. Ethen turned off the lamp, and in the dark the hallway on the plywood disappeared entirely, all its careful converging lines gone at once, and the three of them stood there in the yard listening to the mosquitoes.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
story:
Julia spread the printout on a flat slab of limestone at the edge of the quarry, weighting its corners with four round stones so the wind off the water couldn't take it. The graph showed a single line climbing in steps across a century, small wobbles at first, then a rise so steep it looked like a mistake in the printing. She had chosen the quarry because it was quiet and because nobody from school came here on a Sunday, but Rafaelle had found her anyway, mountain bike dropped in the gravel behind him.

"You're doing the Clarke-Williams thing," he said, looking down at the paper without touching it. "The climate report." He sat on the ledge beside her, close enough that she could smell the sunscreen on his arms. "Jeremie's at home refusing to start his."

"I'm not refusing," she said. "I'm stuck." She pointed at the line. "I can read it. Parts per million, it goes up, faster after 1950. Fine. But he wants us to explain the mechanism, not just describe the graph, and every time I try to say it out loud it turns into a paragraph of nothing. Like I'm quoting something I don't actually own."

Rafaelle squinted at the water below them, green and perfectly still where the excavators had stopped digging years ago. "So explain it to me. I know nothing. I'm a perfect test."

She took a breath. "Sunlight comes through the air and warms the ground, and the ground sends heat back up as infrared. Some gases in the air absorb that heat and keep it from escaping, so the air stays warmer than it would otherwise. That's the greenhouse effect." She paused, waiting for him to object, and when he only nodded she went on. "The problem is that when I say it, I sound like a recording. Mr. Clarke-Williams asked me on Thursday where the idea came from, and I said scientists noticed it recently, and he just looked at me. He does that. He looks at you like the answer is on the floor somewhere and you haven't bent down yet."

"Maybe it is on the floor," Rafaelle said. "Figuratively. Maybe look it up instead of guessing."

She had looked it up, that night, in her room with the window cracked open and the neighbour's television murmuring through the wall, and what she found had unsettled her in a way she couldn't explain to her mother at dinner. "It's not new at all," she said now. "In 1859, a physicist named John Tyndall started doing laboratory experiments, measuring how gases absorb infrared heat. He showed that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it, and nitrogen and oxygen don't." She said it slowly, checking each part against the page she had read three times. "Nitrogen and oxygen are almost all of the air. The gases that trap the heat are the trace ones. He measured that in a lab, with tubes and a thermopile, before there were cars."

Rafaelle was quiet for a while. A kingfisher dropped from the far wall of the quarry, touched the water, and rose again with something silver in its beak. "So the science is old," he said finally, "but the graph is new."

That was it, exactly. Julia felt the two halves of her report slide toward each other. She had been treating the history as decoration, something to parametrize the essay with, a date to slot into the introduction like a coordinate on an axis, while the real work happened later in the data. But Tyndall's tubes were the reason anyone knew what to measure. Without the lab result, the rising line on her printout would just be a line. "I had it backwards," she said. "I thought the past was the background and the graph was the argument. They're the same argument. The air's been the same air the whole time; we just changed how much of the absorbing part is in it." She said "absorbing part" and heard how careful it was, and decided she liked the carefulness. She was not ready to say more than she could defend.

"Jeremie's going to write twelve pages," Rafaelle said. "You know how he gets. Prolix, that's the word. He used it about himself once, proud of it." He picked up one of her corner stones and turned it over in his fingers. "He's also convinced the whole report is political, that Clarke-Williams only assigns it because he's some kind of dissident."

"He's not a dissident," Julia said. "He's a chemistry teacher who owns too many cardigans. The Tyndall thing settles that, actually. You can't be a rebel for believing something measured in 1859." Though even as she said it, she wondered whether that was entirely true. Plenty of people disputed the graph anyway, and she couldn't say precisely why, or what would change their minds, or whether a mechanism this simple had ever felt this hard to hold. She said so out loud, because keeping it inside had been the problem all week. "What I still don't get is what I'm allowed to be uncertain about and what I just have to know cold."

They worked through the afternoon. Rafaelle made her explain the greenhouse effect four more times, and each telling got shorter and plainer, until by the last one it was three sentences and he could repeat it back correctly without looking at the printout. She folded the graph along its creases and put it in her backpack, and they climbed the gravel path to the road while the light went long and amber across the quarry walls. At the top Rafaelle got back on his bike and pushed off, then braked and looked back at her.

"Tell Jeremie about Tyndall," he said. "Tell him the cars are new and the air isn't."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
The parking lot behind the gym had been repainted with fresh yellow lines that morning, and Coralie stood on one of them as though it were the edge of a stage, her trumpet hanging at her side. The band was scattered across the asphalt in loose rows, waiting for Mr. Whitaker to finish arguing with the sound man, and the June heat rose off the hoods of the teachers' cars in visible ribbons. In three hours they would play for her own graduation, which felt like being asked to wait on tables at her own wedding.

"Why is it always this one?" she asked, lifting the trumpet. "Every school in the country. Every movie. Somebody chose it, right? Somebody had to be first."

Moses shrugged the way he shrugged at most questions, but Marwa, who read trivia the way other people read horoscopes, was already pulling her phone out of her uniform pocket. "Okay, hold on. There's a whole thing." She scrolled, shielding the screen from the glare. "It got played at Yale's commencement in 1905. That's where it started being graduation music. Edward Elgar was there getting an honorary doctorate of music, and they played his march, and after that it just spread."

"Elgar wrote it," Coralie said. It was not a question. She had played the piece eleven times in four years and had never once asked whose melody she was carrying. The opening bars had begun to beguile her again this week, the way familiar music does, slipping past her impatience before she could raise a defense against it.

Mr. Whitaker clapped his hands and called them to order, and the lot filled with the slow, processional sound. Halfway through, he cut them off. "Affective," he said, tapping his chest. "I want it affective, not just loud. This is the last thing these families hear before their kids stop being kids." Coralie privately thought this was the sort of aphorism adults produce at ceremonies, a sentence built to be quoted rather than believed, but she adjusted her embouchure anyway and played the phrase softer, and it did sound better, which annoyed her.

During the water break, Marwa sat on the bumper of a gray sedan that belonged to nobody they knew. "It's weird," Marwa said. "A song for one man's award becomes the song for everybody's, forever. Millions of kids walking to something Elgar never heard of." Coralie turned the idea over. She had spent four years wanting to be original, distinctive, the player Mr. Whitaker pointed to, and now she was about to walk to a piece of music chosen by an accident in 1905, along with everyone she knew, and something in her found that not humiliating but almost tender. To be sent off with the same notes as everybody else. To want, still, to play them better.

"You could fight it," Moses offered. "You could refuse to walk to it."

"Then I'd just be the girl who didn't walk," Coralie said. "That's not original, either. That's the same costume worn backwards."

When the ceremony came, the chairs on the football field faced a stage stacked with speakers, and Coralie, in her gown and stole, sat in the third row while a recording of Pomp and Circumstance poured out of the sound system, immaculate and slightly too slow. Mr. Whitaker had cut the live band that afternoon; the sound man had insisted, something about levels, and there had been no time to argue. So she rose with her row and moved toward the stage under Elgar's melody played by musicians who were not there, her trumpet locked in the band room, her fingers moving against her thigh in the fingerings anyway.

Her name was called. She crossed the stage, shook hands, received the folder with the certificate inside, and descended on the far side, where Marwa was waiting with her own folder and a look of suppressed laughter. "We rehearsed for nothing," Marwa said.

Coralie looked back at the field, at the next row already standing, at the borrowed music carrying them forward. "Play me something," she said, and held out her hand for Marwa's folder. "Anything. Just not this."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historiography is the study of how history has been written, including how historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time.
story:
Coralie had two textbooks open on the desk beside her keyboard, and the cat was doing its best to abscond with the strip of paper she was using as a bookmark, sliding it out inch by inch while she typed. She let it go. The bookmark was the least of her problems.

The assignment, posted by Ms. Kerr that morning, was straightforward enough: "Choose one historical event and explain how accounts of it differ across sources." What was not straightforward was the stack of evidence her grandmother had left on the porch in a shoebox last weekend, after finally clearing out the attic. On top of the box sat a school textbook from 1961, its cover gone soft, its pages the colour of weak tea. Coralie's own textbook, two feet away, was a bright slab of current edition, and the two of them told the story of the same war the way two witnesses might describe the same car crash: overlapping, but angled.

She typed a line, deleted it, typed it again. On the other monitor, her chemistry notes sat half-finished, a formula for enthalpy glowing in the middle of the screen, waiting for her to get back to it. Everything was waiting for her to get back to it.

Her phone buzzed. Jeff, from the group chat: "anyone started Kerr's thing yet. asking for me."

She called him instead of texting back, wedging the phone between her ear and shoulder. "I have my grandmother's textbook," she said. "From when she was in school. It's about the war we're studying."

"So use it. Old book, new book, done."

"It's not that simple. The old book basically gives the whole thing one paragraph. Big picture, leaders, dates, everyone united at home. My book has three chapters and half of it is about arguments, people who disagreed, stuff that got left out of the newspapers at the time. Jeff, they're not just different lengths. They're different stories."

There was a pause, and she could hear him eating something. "So which one's right?"

That was the question, and the fact that she couldn't answer it in one word was what had kept her at the desk for two hours. "I don't think it works like that," she said slowly. "The old book wasn't lying. It was written by people who could only see what they could see. Their sources were partial. And then the questions people ask change, later, so historians go looking for different things, and the history gets rewritten." She heard herself say it and felt the small click of it fitting together, the way a formula finally balances. "It has a name, I think. Hang on."

She put Jeff on speaker and searched. It took three tries to find the term, buried in a university page she'd clicked through from a footnote, and when she found it she said it out loud so it would stick. "Historiography. It's the study of how history has been written, including how historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time."

"Say that five times fast," said Jeff.

"Historiography." She wrote it at the top of a fresh page, then underlined the date on the inside cover of her grandmother's book, 1961, and beside it wrote the publication date of her own. Two points on a line. Between them, decades of new letters found in attics, new questions, new people deciding that certain voices counted as sources at all.

The doorbell rang, and it was Terry, who lived three doors down and had walked over because Coralie's mother had mentioned she was buried in homework. Terry flopped onto the bed, looked at the sedimentary layers spread across the desk, old book under new book under printed articles under the cat, and said, "This looks like a geology dig."

"It kind of is." Coralie turned the laptop so Terry could see the screen. "Look. Same event, two books, sixty years apart. In the old one, the home front is one sentence about everyone pulling together. In mine, there's a whole section on the strikes, on people who were locked up, on the fights over what the war was even for." She scrolled. "And here's the part I can't shake. When my grandmother was my age, she read this and believed it, the way I believe mine. In sixty years, somebody might read my textbook and see everything that's missing from it."

"Depressing," said Terry.

"It's the opposite, actually." Coralie pulled the keyboard toward her. "It means history isn't a wall you hit and that's it. It's still being argued about, which means people are still looking. Still finding shoeboxes in attics." She glanced at the box on the floor, its contents half-excavated, a bundle of her great-grandfather's letters still tied in string at the bottom. "I'm going to use those. Primary sources, from the actual year. Maybe they agree with the old book. Maybe they don't. Maybe I won't be able to tell."

Terry picked up the old textbook and turned to the single paragraph, reading it with the mild suspicion of someone checking a receipt. "You're going to get a good grade on this," Terry said, "and I'm going to get a C, because my comparative sources are two websites that look exactly the same."

"Come here, then," Coralie said, and pulled out the second chair, and untied the string on the letters, and offered Terry the first one.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The phone repair shop smelled of solder and lemon cleaner, and Alexandra had been standing at the counter for ten minutes while the technician peeled the back off her phone. She had come in for a cracked screen. What she left with was something else entirely, though she didn't know that yet.

On the wall-mounted television behind the register, a muted news loop showed a clip of a flooded street, a bus half-submerged, people wading with bags held over their heads. The caption scrolled: LOCAL? VIDEO CLAIMS TO SHOW DOWNTOWN FLOODING. Alexandra leaned toward the screen. She had seen that exact video an hour ago, shared by her aunt with three exclamation points and the words "this is five minutes from your school." Her school was five minutes from nothing but a cornfield.

"Do you mind if I ask you something?" she said to the technician, a wiry man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead. "That flood video. Can you tell where it's from?"

He glanced up. "Depends who's asking."

"A person who almost sent it to forty people," Alexandra said.

He laughed. Behind him, waiting on her own repaired charger port, sat Darien from her media studies class, hunched over a coffee. He raised the cup in salute.

That was how it started. Darien slid over, pulled out his laptop, and said the words that rearranged her whole afternoon: "You know you can't just search a video backwards, right? Most image search engines won't take a video at all." Alexandra stared at him. She had assumed, without ever articulating it, that a search box was a search box; you fed it a thing and it found the thing. The idea that a moving image might be invisible to the tools she used every day felt like discovering a door she'd leaned on for years was painted on the wall.

"So what do actual fact-checkers do," she asked, "just give up?"

"They screenshot it." Darien spun the laptop toward her. "Key frames, still moments. You pause the video, grab the image, and search that instead." He demonstrated on a different clip, a burning warehouse: pause, screenshot, drag the image into the search bar. Results bloomed, all of them dated two years earlier and an ocean away. "See," he said. "The video lies about its own birthday."

The technician handed Alexandra her phone back, its screen whole and gleaming, and refused her money twice before accepting it once. "You two should teach a class," he said. "The number of people who come in here showing me videos, asking me if the phone's broken because the truth won't load." He was joking, mostly, but Alexandra had met that type: her aunt, who had once been briefly famous in the family group chat for a video of a shark swimming down a highway that turned out to be from a movie. The family had forgiven it as a small peccadillo, the way they forgave her uncle's irascible commentary on referees, but Alexandra wondered now whether forgiveness was the wrong instrument entirely. A mistake shared once is a mistake. A mistake shared by forty people is a small weather system.

She went home and tried it herself, pausing the flood video at the moment a man in a red jacket turned toward the camera, cropping the frame, searching the image. The results were in Portuguese. The flood was real, the man was real, his jacket was real, and every one of them had existed in a different country fourteen months before the caption claimed.

Here is what Darien texted her that night, while she sat cross-legged on her bed surrounded by screenshots: "Okay I have a confession. I only knew about the frame thing because I fell for a video last spring. A clip of a politician saying something horrible. I sent it to our whole group chat before Hiba told me it was cut. I felt like an idiot for a week. Then I decided if the tools could incapacitate my judgment that easily, I should probably learn how the tools actually work. Anyway. Nice work on the flood thing. You were faster than me."

Alexandra read it three times. She had been thinking of him as the person who knew things, and he had been quietly recasting himself as the person who had once not known things, which was a different and somehow more useful category. She typed, then deleted, then typed: "Did you ever tell the group chat you were wrong?" His reply came after a long pause: "I told Hiba."

She drafted her response to her aunt carefully. She attached the screenshot of the man in the red jacket, the Portuguese headline, the date. She wrote that the flood was real, and that this was somehow the confusing part: nothing in the video was false except its claim to be happening here, now, to us. She asked her aunt, gently, whether a thing could be true and still be a lie. Then she hesitated over the send button, because she didn't actually know the answer, and didn't want to pretend she did. She sent it anyway.

The next morning the video had been shared again in the family group chat, this time by her cousin, with the caption "so scary!!" attached, and beneath it, from her aunt, a single line: "I checked, it's from Brazil, please stop sharing." Alexandra stared at the thread, then at her own message sitting unanswered just above it, timestamped eleven hours earlier. Then she screenshotted the whole exchange, and started searching it.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
story:
Emile had the marble slab balanced across two arms of the kitchen sink because it wouldn't fit anywhere else, and it was cold in the way that made his wrists ache, which was the whole point. "You're going to give me salmonella," Jared said from the doorway, though the real risk, as far as Emile understood it, was something worse: dull, soft chocolate that bent instead of snapping, the kind that sweats grey streaks and disappoints everyone who touches it.

The trouble had started two weeks earlier at Lilia's house, where her mother kept a long stone counter by the window that stayed cold even in August. Lilia had been melting chocolate for a birthday thing, and Emile, waiting for her to finish so they could walk to the bus, had watched her pour the melted chocolate onto the stone and spread it back and forth with a spatula, gathering it and spreading it again, patient as someone folding laundry. "It's called tabling," she'd said, not looking up. "You work it on the cold stone until it cools down. That's what makes it set right." He'd asked how she knew when it was done, and she'd said she just knew, by the way it thickened, and that answer had bothered him for days, the way answers without reasons always did.

At home his first attempt had failed in the microwave, which was a sentence he hadn't known a person could say. The chocolate seized into a grainy paste, and his mother had stood in the kitchen doorway holding a grocery bag and observing that he was making a mess of something she hadn't known he cared about. She wasn't wrong. He had signed up to make truffles for Ms. Owusu's farewell thing on Friday, mostly because Lilia had mentioned offhandedly that nobody else had volunteered, and then had felt trapped by his own yes, a small familiar trap he kept walking into. He'd also, in a fit of either ambition or spite, promised they'd have a proper snap.

The second attempt, tempering by seeding, followed a video whose narrator spoke in the calm voice of a man narrating golf. Emile stirred melted chocolate with chopped chocolate in a bowl, watching the thermometer, and the numbers behaved, and the result still bloomed grey overnight. He'd sat at the kitchen table at one in the morning turning the failed batch over under the light like a jeweler, or like a teenager with no jewelry and one bar of ruined chocolate, which was closer to the truth. It was during that night, or the grey part of the morning after, that he thought of the stone counter at Lilia's. Not marble, but cold, and stone, and the cold was the part he'd been missing.

So he'd bought the slab with the money from tutoring, and now the kitchen smelled like warm chocolate, and the double boiler was ticking softly on the stove. Jared had come over because he claimed to want to learn, though so far his contribution was commentary. "If this works," Jared said, "you owe me a truffle for emotional support." Emile poured a pool of melted chocolate onto the marble, and the warmth of it against the cold stone made a small cloud of chocolate smell rise up, and he began spreading it out thin with the spatula, then scraping it back into the center, out and back, out and back.

It was strange work. His chemistry teacher, not Ms. Owusu, a different teacher whose name Emile had let atrophy years ago into just "Mr. Chem," would have called it crystallization and drawn arrows. Lilia called it knowing by feel. Both were true, he thought, working the chocolate, and both were insufficient alone, which was itself a kind of truism he was starting to distrust, since saying both sides are partly right was sometimes just a way of not choosing. The chocolate moved differently now, thickening, holding the ridges of the spatula for a half second before relaxing flat. He pressed the back of his knuckle against a smeared edge to test it. Body temperature was the test, Lilia had said; when the chocolate stops feeling cool against your lip, it's close. He didn't put his lip on the counter with Jared watching, so his knuckle would have to serve.

"That's it," he said, and it came out more uncertain than he wanted, so he said it again with different emphasis. "That's it." He scraped the chocolate back into the bowl with the warm remainder and stirred, and the whole mass moved as one thing now, glossy, and he dipped a knife tip and laid a thin stripe on parchment to test. "This is the part where you wait," he told Jared, "and the waiting is diurnal, like, this could take all night." "That's not what that word means," Jared said. "It means daily. Like a newspaper." "Diurnal rhythms," Emile said. "Look it up." Jared did not look it up; he opened the fridge and ate a pickle, which he claimed was for emotional support also.

Ms. Owusu had once told their class, on a day Emile remembered for no reason he could defend, that the difference between knowing a thing and knowing how to do it was the difference between a map and walking. He had thought it was a line designed for yearbook pages. Standing at the sink, watching a stripe of chocolate decide what it would become, he understood that she'd been describing something specific, though he still couldn't have said whether his map was any good, or whether the walking had taught him the route or only that he was clumsy. The stripe on the parchment had gone matte at the edges and glossy at the center, and when he touched it, it was set, and when he pushed the knife under it, it came up with a click, clean off the paper.

He snapped the test stripe in half and it broke sharp, an actual sound, and Jared said, "Okay, that's weirdly satisfying," and took half without asking. Emile looked at the two pieces of evidence in his hand: a clean break, a shine, and underneath those, a certainty that the next batch might not cooperate, that the slab and the room temperature and the specific chocolate had all been on his side tonight and might not be tomorrow. He wasn't sure he could do it twice. He was sure he'd try, which felt like a different and slightly sturdier thing than confidence.

On Friday he carried the truffles to school in a tin with a rubber band around it, and Ms. Owusu unwrapped one and bit it and paused in the middle of saying goodbye to someone, which was the whole review Emile needed. Near the door Lilia was watching him, and she came over and said, "So the marble actually worked." "Worked once," Emile said. She took a truffle, snapped it beside her ear like she was checking a coin, and said, "Then do it again tonight."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2018 World Cup in Russia was the first to use video assistant referees, who can review goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity.
story:
The living room had been rearranged for the occasion, the couch pulled closer to the television and the good chairs angled in from the kitchen. Michael sat on the floor with his back against the couch's leg, a paper plate balanced on his knee, while his uncle argued with the referee on the screen in a voice loud enough to make the lamp shade tremble. Marley had claimed the armchair an hour before kickoff and refused to give it up. Rylan lay across the carpet with his chin propped on both fists, narrating the passing in a low mutter, as though the players could hear him and would benefit from his advice.

It was the quarterfinal, and France was winning by a single goal in the eighty-seventh minute. Michael's father kept standing up and sitting down again, unable to settle, and Michael understood the impulse completely, because his own pulse would not slow either. Then the striker he had been rooting against all afternoon collected a loose ball in the box and drove it low into the corner, and for three seconds the room detonated. Rylan was on his feet. Marley had both hands in her hair. The uncle's roar drowned out the commentary entirely.

But the linesman's flag stayed down and the referee's hand went to his ear, and then the screen showed the words every fan had learned to dread that summer: the play was under review. "What is he even checking," Rylan said, still standing, though the standing now had a hollow quality to it. "The ball was in. We all saw it."

"They're called video assistant referees," Michael said, not looking up from the screen. He had read about the system before the tournament, in one of those long afternoons when he read anything within reach, and the details had stayed with him the way trivia always did, lodged and permanent. "It's the first World Cup using them. This one, in Russia." He paused, deciding how much to say. "They can look at goals, penalties, straight red cards, and if the referee carded the wrong guy. Mistaken identity."

"So the whole goal might get taken away," Marley said slowly, "because a man in a room somewhere is watching it again."

"Basically, yeah."

The review took almost two minutes. The referee stood at the edge of the pitch with his hand pressed to his ear, and seventy thousand people in the stadium and nine people in the living room waited on his decision. Michael's mother came in from the kitchen with a bowl of grapes nobody wanted and settled on the arm of the couch. The replay ran three times, then four, the same striker's shoulder and the same defender's heel, frame by frame, and Michael found that the waiting had changed something for him. He had grown up on the argument that human error was part of the game, that a blown call was a story you told for years, that the game's whole character was underpinned by its imperfection. His uncle had said so a hundred times, usually about a disallowed goal from 1986.

At the same time, he had spent the school year learning what evidence could do. Mr. Bouchard, his history teacher, had made them re-read sources until the confident version of an event fell apart into something smaller and truer, and Michael had liked that, had liked the discipline of it. certainty felt like a thing you should have to earn. And here was that principle wearing a referee's uniform, rewinding a championship on a grainy screen, and it looked, honestly, terrible. Both positions seemed right. He could not make them agree.

"Offside," the referee announced, and pointed for the free kick, and the goal was gone.

Rylan made a sound like a kettle and dropped back to the carpet. Marley said nothing at all, which from Marley was the loudest possible response. The uncle began a speech about how the game was being ruined, how they had taken something alive and replaced it with something antiseptic, and Michael listened and did not argue, because part of him had been standing in that camp ninety seconds ago. But another part kept returning to the freeze-frame, to the striker's shoulder a half-step beyond the last defender, a fact that had been true whether or not anyone had seen it. The system was new and clumsy and it had made the room miserable. It had also, as far as he could tell, gotten it right, and he could not find the argument that made both of those things false at once.

He thought about asking Mr. Bouchard, in September, how you were supposed to hold two ideas like that without dropping either. He suspected the answer involved the word Mr. Bouchard used for everything complicated, which was "nevertheless," and he suspected it would not help much.

France cleared the free kick, and the clock ran out, and the whistle went. Rylan lay flat on the carpet with his eyes closed. Marley finally spoke. "Same time Sunday," she said, already reaching for the remote.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA calls 4 to 60 degrees Celsius (40 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit) the danger zone, the range where bacteria in food multiply rapidly.
story:
The kitchen of Corvino's closed to customers at ten, but Justin stayed after his shift on Thursdays because Mr. Harper, the owner, had agreed to teach him what his mother called, with a certain flatness, "actual life skills." He was leaving for college in September, eight hundred miles from her kitchen, and he had signed himself up for this. Tonight Mr. Harper set a legal pad on the stainless steel counter between the prep sink and the walk-in and told him to write down seven dinners. Not seven dishes, seven dinners, with sides, with quantities, with a shopping list that accounted for what he already had. Justin wrote "chili" first, because chili was the only thing he could currently make, and Mr. Harper circled it and wrote "2" beside it, meaning two meals, meaning leftovers, meaning the whole point of batching.

That had been three weeks ago. Since then Justin had learned to plan a week on Sunday, shop on Monday when the store was empty, and cook in long slow afternoons in Mr. Harper's kitchen: one vat of chili, one tray of roasted chicken thighs, one pot of rice that would become fried rice on Wednesday. Mr. Harper was not sentimental about any of it. "Cooking is logistics," he said. He had a pithy saying for nearly every stage, and Justin had started keeping them in the back of the notebook, an adage per page, because some of them were genuinely useful and some were just things a tired man says at midnight.

The trouble came on a Friday in July. Justin had made his chili at Mr. Harper's, a double batch, and carried the pot home on the bus with a towel folded over the lid. He set it on the counter to cool. Then Faris called from the pickup court, and then they lost track of time at the gas station buying slushies, and then Justin got home at one in the morning and his mother was asleep and he was asleep almost before he was horizontal. The pot sat on the counter all night, lid on, in a kitchen that had not cooled down with the July dark.

He noticed it at nine. It was still warm, faintly, when he lifted the lid, and he stood there with a spoon in his hand doing the arithmetic he did not yet know how to do. Mary had stayed over, having crashed in the basement after the slushie detour, and she came up behind him with her hair still flattened from the couch cushions.

"Is that the chili from last night?" she said.

"It's fine," Justin said, though he had not decided yet whether it was.

"You left it out all night?"

"Cooked food, lid on. It's basically a can." He could hear how much he wanted that to be true. Mary took out her phone, and he watched her type, and he watched her face while she read, and he resented the whole sequence.

"It's called the danger zone," she said. "Four to sixty degrees Celsius. Forty to one hundred forty Fahrenheit. That's the range where bacteria multiply rapidly, and it's, like, the official thing, it's the USDA."

"The USDA has opinions about my chili."

"The USDA has opinions about everything you eat." She turned the screen toward him and he read it himself, twice, the numbers stubborn and specific, the word danger doing exactly the work it was designed to do. He thought about throwing it out, and the thought had a particular weight, because the chili was four meals, four meals of money he had earned bussing tables, and he thought about his mother's grocery budget when he was eleven and the year the fridge died and how she had made him a game of it, cooking everything before it spoiled, one marathon Saturday. She had lost a whole tray of chicken that day anyway and had not said a word about it, just washed the tray, and he had understood even then that the silence was the price being counted.
